ABSTRACT
This study highlights the synergistic integration of titanium dioxide (TiO
2
) with microwave-exfoliated reduced 
graphene oxide (ME-rGO) for advanced supercapacitor and sensing applications. The TiO
2 
content in the hybrid 
nanocomposite was systematically optimized to maximize performance for diverse applications. ME-rGO was 
synthesized through a combined microwave-assisted and modified Hummer ’ s route, enabling a highly conduc -
tive and defect-engineered nanocomposite. Additionally, the nanocomposites were characterized using various 
techniques, including X-ray diffraction (XRD), field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), Fourier- 
transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and Raman spectroscopy. Electrochemical investigation revealed that 
the ME-rGO/TiO
2 
nanocomposite (TR-10) delivered a specific capacitance of 156 Fg
� 1
, nearly double that of 
pristine ME-rGO. This enhancement arises from the synergistic effect of the electric double-layer capacitance 
contributed by ME-rGO and the pseudocapacitive effect contributed by TiO
2
. The optimized TR-10 exhibited an 
excellent energy density of 7.8 Wh kg
� 1
, a power density 1.6 kW/kg and excellent cyclic stability with 94.2 % 
capacitance retention after 5000 charge-discharge cycles. The nanocomposite has also been used for the sensing 
of dopamine, and the LOD of 2.9 μ M was achieved. In conclusion, this research demonstrates the efficacy of 
metallic oxide ‑ carbon nanomaterial hybrids in producing high-performance, multifunctional electrodes, thereby 
opening up opportunities for the large-scale manufacturing of future energy storage and sensor devices.
1. Introduction
With the rapid advancement of next-generation electronics and 
portable energy devices, there has been a growing demand for advanced, 
multifunctional materials that can perform two key functions: energy 
storage and chemical or biosensing interfaces. In these situations, 
bifunctional electrode materials have emerged as strong contenders, 
specifically those with high electrochemical performance, coupled with 
molecular recognition and sensitivity in detection. [ 1 – 6 ] The two-way 
capability of such a feature is instrumental in system integration 
design, particularly for wearable electronics, implantable devices, and 
smart sensors, where component miniaturization is necessary without 
compromising versatility. Supercapacitors, also known as 
electrochemical capacitors, are best recognized for their high-power 
density, long cycle life, and fast charge-discharge capabilities. Their 
energy density typically lags behind that of batteries. [ 7 ] To enhance 
performance and multifunctionality, scientists have increasingly tar -
geted nanostructured materials with pseudocapacitive responses, high 
redox activity, and high surface areas for interaction with the electro -
lyte. [ 3 , 8 – 12 ] However, electrochemical sensors require materials with 
improved electrical conductivity, surface reactivity, and chemical 
selectivity. Creating a material that performs both functions efficiently is 
a synergistic combination of high conductivity, electroactive surface 
sites, and structural stability.
Reduced graphene oxide (rGO), which is a derivative of graphene, is 
among the most interesting materials in this group. Its superior

properties, including a high theoretical surface area (~2630 m
2
/g), high 
carrier mobility, chemical stability, and tunable surface chemistry, make 
it an ideal backbone for hybrid architectures. [ 13 ] In addition, its oxy -
gen functionalities and intrinsic defects not only contribute capacitance 
through faradaic mechanisms but also provide active sites and binding 
sites for sensing purposes. [ 14 – 19 ] Among all the synthesis routes, 
microwave-exfoliation has been of particular interest as a rapid, envi -
ronmentally friendly, and scalable method to synthesize rGO sheets with 
reduced layer numbers, high defects, and intact conjugated networks. 
[ 20 , 21 ] The rapid dielectric heating in the microwave process causes 
thermal shock-induced exfoliation, which prevents restacking and fa -
vors the development of defect-rich rGO with high electrical conduc -
tivity. The method also enables homogeneous heating and rapid reaction 
kinetics, making it highly desirable for heat and sensor devices.
However, despite its advantageous properties, rGO-based electrodes 
often exhibit limited specific capacitance, mainly due to the restacking 
of graphene layers and the absence of faradaic reactions, which restricts 
their energy storage capacity. To overcome these limitations, developing 
hybrid materials that combine the high conductivity and surface area of 
rGO with the pseudocapacitive behaviour of transition metal oxides has 
gained considerable interest. Transition metal oxides, such as MnO ₂ , 
NiO, Co ₃ O ₄ , and TiO ₂ [ 22 – 24 ], offer high theoretical capacitance due to 
their ability to undergo fast and reversible redox reactions. Among 
these, titanium dioxide (TiO ₂ ) is particularly attractive due to its low 
cost, abundance, non-toxicity, environmental compatibility, and chem -
ical stability. [ 25 ] Although TiO ₂ alone suffers from low electrical con -
ductivity, when combined with conductive carbon-based materials, such 
as rGO, it can contribute significantly to enhanced electrochemical 
performance through synergistic effects. [ 26 – 28 ]
In this communication, we try to test the same nanocomposite ma -
terial for two distinct applications: supercapacitor and sensors. It dem -
onstrates its multifunctionality and real-world practicality. For the 
reduction of graphene oxide (GO), a microwave-assisted method was 
employed. This technique is a highly efficient approach, achieving rapid 
exfoliation within seconds, whereas conventional reduction methods 
typically require several hours.
A microwave-exfoliated reduced graphene oxide/titanium dioxide 
(ME-rGO/TiO ₂ ) nanocomposite was synthesized and employed as a 
bifunctional electrode material for energy storage and sensing applica -
tions. The morphology, structure, and surface chemistry of the ME-rGO/ 
TiO ₂ composite were investigated using X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Fourier 
Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Field-Emission Scanning 
Electron Microscopy (FESEM), and Raman spectroscopy, demonstrating 
successful exfoliation and composite formation. The capacitive perfor -
mance was evaluated through electrochemical analyses, including cyclic 
voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), and electro -
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The composite exhibited a high 
specific capacitance, good rate performance, and excellent cycle life, 
demonstrating potential as a suitable material for high-performance 
supercapacitors. Furthermore, its sensing capability was also exam -
ined using a model redox analyte, dopamine (DA), in which case the 
composite electrode exhibited high sensitivity, low detection limit, and 
satisfactory selectivity. Apart from enhancing the fundamental under -
standing of interfacial synergy between rGO and TiO ₂ , this research 
suggests a novel approach to the synthesis of bifunctional nanohybrids 
for integrated electrochemical devices. The ME-rGO is used here as a 
conducting but defective matrix, while the addition of TiO ₂ disrupts both 
redox sites and analyte adsorption capability. Combined, these features 
make the ME-rGO/TiO ₂ hybrid a perfect candidate for electrochemical 
dual-purpose devices. The synergistic effect of these attributes makes the 
ME-rGO/TiO ₂ hybrid a promising material for dual-purpose electro -
chemical devices.

2.2. Synthesis of graphite oxide
In a typical synthesis, 5 g of graphite powder was added to 250 mL of 
concentrated sulfuric acid (H ₂ SO ₄ ) in a reaction vessel, and the mixture 
was stirred to ensure a uniform dispersion. Subsequently, 2.5 g of so -
dium nitrate (NaNO ₃ ) was introduced into the mixture, and the

suspension was stirred continuously overnight to promote intercalation 
and reaction between the components. Following this, 20 g of potassium 
permanganate (KMnO
4
) was added gradually to the reaction mixture 
over 4 – 5 h, maintaining continuous stirring. The slow addition was 
crucial in controlling the exothermic reaction and preventing a rapid 
temperature rise. As the oxidation progressed, the mixture turned 
greenish, indicating the formation of intermediate manganese- 
containing species and the onset of graphite oxidation. After complete 
addition of KMnO
4
, the mixture was stirred overnight at room temper -
ature to ensure complete oxidation and formation of graphite oxide. 
Subsequently, 100 mL of deionized water (DI) was added dropwise to 
the mixture. This step caused a noticeable colour change from greenish 
to brown, indicating further oxidation and exfoliation of the graphite 
layers. To terminate the reaction and reduce residual permanganate and 
manganese dioxide, hydrogen peroxide (H ₂ O ₂ ) was added, resulting in a 
bright yellow coloration of the suspension. To remove residual acids and 
metal ions, the reaction mixture was diluted with an additional 400 mL 
of DI water. The resulting solution was then subjected to multiple 
washing steps. First, it was rinsed with a 10 % HCl solution to eliminate 
metal ion impurities. This was followed by repeated washing with 
distilled water until the filtrate reached a neutral pH (between 7 and 9), 
indicating the effective removal of acidic and basic residues. The 
resulting purified product was identified as graphite oxide (GO), ready 
for further processing. The schematic process of GO synthesis is given in 
Fig. 1a .
2.3. Synthesis of microwave exfoliated reduced Graphene Oxide (ME- 
rGO)
To reduce, GO to reduced graphene oxide (rGO), the synthesized GO 
is placed in an alumina crucible within a microwave. The power of the 
microwave oven is set to 100 % (high), and the sample is subjected to 
microwave heating. The timing of microwave irradiation is carefully 
noted for 5 min. During the process, it is observed that the exfoliation of 
the GO occurs rapidly, taking only 120 s for complete exfoliation to 
occur. This rapid exfoliation indicates the efficient reduction of GO to 
rGO. As a result of the exfoliation, the rGO becomes suspended in the air 
within the crucible, signifying the commencement of the exfoliation 
process. This observation highlights the efficacy of microwave irradia -
tion as a method for preparing reduced graphene oxide.
2.4. Synthesis of ME-rGO/TiO
2
To synthesize the ME-rGO/TiO ₂ composite ( Fig. 1b ), 45 mg of 
microwave-exfoliated reduced graphene oxide (ME-rGO) was dispersed 
in 45 mL of ethanol and sonicated for 15 min to ensure uniform 
dispersion. Separately, 5 mg of titanium dioxide (TiO ₂ ) nanoparticles 
were dispersed in 5 mL of ethanol and also sonicated for 15 min to 
achieve a homogeneous suspension. The TiO ₂ dispersion was then added 
dropwise to the ME-rGO suspension under continuous stirring. The 
resulting mixture was stirred and heated simultaneously for 6 h to 
facilitate the interaction and integration of TiO ₂ onto the ME-rGO sur -
face. After the stirring process was completed, the composite mixture 
was transferred to an oven and dried at temperature (60 
◦
C) for 3 h to 
obtain the final ME-rGO/TiO ₂ composite material in powder form, for 
making different samples with varying TiO
2 
weights of 5 mg, 10 mg, and 
15 mg, respectively, and named as TR-5, TR-10, and TR-15.
2.5. Physicochemical characterization
The crystallinity of the synthesized materials was analyzed using X- 
ray diffraction (XRD) with a Panalytical Xpert Pro diffractometer, 
employing a CuK
α 
radiation source ( λ = 1.5406 Å). Surface morphology 
and microstructural features were examined using a field emission 
scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Merlin Compact, Carl Zeiss). 
Raman spectroscopy was performed using a JASCO NRS spectrometer to 
evaluate the structural integrity and defect states of the graphene-based 
materials. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was per -
formed using a PerkinElmer Spectrum Two spectrometer to identify 
functional groups and assess the molecular composition of the samples.
2.6. Electrochemical characterization
Electrochemical testing was conducted using an electrochemical 
workstation (CHI 760). A symmetric cell configuration employing a two- 
electrode system was utilized for the testing process. To prepare the 
electrodes, a slurry containing ME-rGO, Acetylene Black, and Poly -
vinylidene Fluoride (PVDF) in a ratio of 8:1:1, dissolved in N-Methyl-2- 
Pyrolidone (NMP), was formulated. The slurry was then coated onto 
nickel foam substrates with a diameter of 14 mm (1 cm
